claims.text: High-entropy alloys can exhibit high corrosion resistance.
High-entropy alloys can exhibit enhanced mechanical properties.
Inherent chemical heterogeneity in high-entropy alloys promotes formation of a stable, self-healing passive layer.
The self-healing passive layer retards aggressive chemical attack.
The passive layer reinforces the surface against mechanical strain through enhanced solid-solution strengthening.
A single-phase AlxCoCrFeNi alloy with a homogeneous BCC or FCC microstructure can form a protective passive film under service conditions.
Preferential oxidation of selected elemental constituents produces a thin, stable passive layer.
Nanoscale precipitates or chemically short-range-ordered regions may aid passive-layer formation or stability.
The multielement composition creates local bonding variations that cause certain elements to oxidize preferentially.
The passive film blocks oxidation and ion penetration and thereby slows corrosion kinetics.
Solid-solution strengthening inherent to high-entropy alloys resists plastic deformation under mechanical load.
Resistance to plastic deformation from solid-solution strengthening reduces wear.
The combination of passive-film protection and enhanced bulk strength makes combined wear-corrosion degradation lower than the sum of isolated wear and corrosion damage.
An HEA with effective passive-film formation will have lower corrosion depth under simultaneous wear and corrosion than a matched baseline with impaired film formation or diminished strengthening.
An HEA with effective passive-film formation will have lower wear volume under simultaneous wear and corrosion than the matched baseline.
The protective effect should hold when passive-film regeneration is faster than mechanical film removal.
The protective effect may fail when mechanical stress or medium aggressiveness causes continuous film removal faster than self-healing.
Controlled oxidation promotes passive-film formation, whereas laser ablation can disrupt or delay it.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes mechanical reinforcement to the passive layer through solid-solution strengthening, whereas the mechanism attributes solid-solution strengthening to the bulk alloy as a separate contribution from the passive film.

The baseline is described as being subjected separately to wear and corrosion, while the predicted comparison and falsification experiment require a matched baseline tested under simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions.
